title: Astronaut Donald Pettit Reveals Changes in City Lights and NASA
seoTitle: Pettit reveals city light changes, NASA crew shift
subtitle: From the night sky to the Moon, two stories that explain the growing interest in astronauts
excerpt: From the record of urban lights changing color from the ISS to the departure of the commander and pilot of the Artemis II mission, NASA is living moments that put a.
author: Daniele Morais
sourceName: Meteored Brasil, Diário do Litoral, SpaceMoney
contentHtml:
In recent weeks, two astronaut-related stories have dominated the headlines: astronaut Donald Roy Pettit posted night‑time image comparisons showing the replacement of sodium‑vapor lamps with LEDs, and NASA announced the departure of commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover from the Artemis II mission, requiring a new crew organization.

How Cities Change Color from Space

During four missions to the International Space Station, Pettit photographed cities around the world. The first images, taken during Expedition 6 (2002‑2003), showed the typical yellow‑orange glow of sodium‑vapor lamps. In September 2024, during Expedition 71‑72, he captured the same urban area with predominantly white and multicolored lighting, reflecting the adoption of LEDs.

The astronaut used an improvised “barn door tracker” to compensate for the ISS’s orbital motion and achieve longer exposures without blurring the lights. Recent comparisons, such as Miami between 2012 and 2025, highlight the global transition to LEDs, which NASA also cites in its light‑pollution studies.

Why the Lighting Change Matters

Beyond aesthetics, the technology shift informs energy decisions: LEDs are more efficient, allow intensity control, and reduce maintenance costs. Pettit’s photographs help scientists analyze urban expansion, population distribution, and energy‑consumption patterns, complementing data from specialized satellites.

However, the increase in white brightness presents challenges for astronomical observation and ecosystems, as excess light hampers star visibility from urban areas.

NASA Loses Commander and Pilot of Artemis II

Reid Wiseman, commander, and Victor Glover, pilot, left the active astronaut roster before the Orion test flight scheduled for Artemis II. Both were announced as responsible for leading the trajectory that skirts the Moon, operating the ship’s main systems, and ensuring a safe re‑entry.

The departure creates a “symbolic and operational void” in the mission, as the duo had already accumulated joint training in simulators, medical exams, and public presentations. Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen remain on the original list, but NASA has yet to announce who will fill the commander and pilot roles.

Impacts of the Crew Reorganization

Crews are formed years in advance; swapping two key members requires a new training phase, recalibration of procedures, and schedule adjustments. The Johnson Space Center in Houston will keep simulators running, flight physicians on duty, and trajectory teams reassessing safety margins.

Although the change does not halt the Artemis program, it underscores the need to adapt the “human texture” of the next launch, maintaining confidence in the hardware (SLS and Orion) and the return plan to the lunar environment.

What the Brazilian Public Can Observe

NASA launches are streamed live and generate great interest in Brazil. Pettit’s images, shared on X, show how urban lighting evolves from a space perspective, while the Artemis II reorganization reminds viewers that the faces seen on broadcasts may change before the rocket ignites.

Thus, the focus on astronaut figures reflects both technological advances—from LEDs to the Orion ship—and the internal dynamics of agencies driving the missions. The near future promises new nighttime Earth images and, possibly, the next crewed lunar‑orbit flight with a new command duo.

With information from Meteored Brasil, Diário do Litoral, SpaceMoney.
